Cusco. The capital and spiritual heart of the Inca Empire, situated high in the Peruvian Andes. Founded according to legend by Manco Capac, it served as the administrative and ceremonial center from which the Incas governed their vast domain. The city's strategic location, sophisticated urban planning, and role as the seat of the Sapa Inca made it the undisputed center of one of pre-Columbian America's greatest civilizations.

Located in the southern highlands of Peru at an elevation of over eleven thousand feet, Cusco is one of the highest cities in the world. It served as the capital of the Inca Empire from its founding until the Spanish conquest in the early sixteenth century. The name Cusco, also spelled Cuzco, means "navel of the world" in Quechua, reflecting its central importance to Incan cosmology. Built on a site the Incas believed was sacred, with origin myths connecting it to the wanderings of Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo.

The city featured sophisticated urban planning organized in a grid pattern, with Manco Capac's palace at the center. The Temple of the Sun, called Qorikancha, was Cusco's most important religious structure, housing gold-plated walls and sacred objects. The city housed the royal court and served as the base for the Sapa Inca's imperial administration across the vast empire. Cusco was largely destroyed by Spanish conquistadors under Pizarro but was incorporated into the Spanish colonial city that still stands today.

Connected to the wider empire through Qhapaq Ñan, the vast network of roads radiating from Cusco to all four quarters of Tawantinsuyu. The city served as both a ceremonial center where imperial rituals occurred and a practical administrative hub for collecting tributes and managing provinces. Archaeological evidence shows Cusco housed elite craft workers, priests, military officials, and merchants, making it a cosmopolitan center for the empire.
